sections.title: Costumbres
sections.summary: Kisses, late arrivals, long goodbyes and a very full calendar

classes.title: Hello, with a kiss
classes.summary: One kiss, everybody, every time

pages.text: In Argentina you say hi with **un beso**: one kiss, cheek to cheek, lips to the air. Not two like in Spain. Just one, and quick.

pages.prompt: Two Argentine guys, old friends, meet at a bar. How do they say hi?
options: A quick nod and a smile
pages.explain: Often a kiss plus a pat on the back, or a hug. Brothers, fathers and sons too. A handshake is for people you barely know.

pages.text: Arrive at a dinner of twelve and you **saludás uno por uno**: you go around and kiss each person, strangers included. A wave from the door feels cold. At a huge party, kiss the people near you.
Which side? Lean to your left, so right cheeks touch. And when you leave, you do the whole round again, with a **chau** for each person.

pages.prompt: Your first week at a new job in Buenos Aires. How do your coworkers greet you in the morning?
pages.explain: In many offices it's a kiss, every morning, often even with the boss. Not everywhere, so watch what others do. Nobody thinks it's intimate. It's just hello.

pages.text: The exception: a very formal first meeting, like a job interview. Then it's often a handshake. Watch what the other person does. By the second meeting, it's usually a kiss.
Then comes **¿Todo bien?** or **¿Qué hacés?** It looks like “what are you doing?” but here it only means hi. Answer **“Todo bien, ¿y vos?”**, not what you are doing.
Meeting someone new at a party? Lean in, kiss, and say your name: **“Hola, soy Sam.”** That's all anyone expects.

classes.title: Argentine time
classes.summary: Late arrivals, loose plans and goodbyes that never end

pages.text: Invited to dinner at someone's home **a las nueve**? Nobody expects you at nine. Twenty or thirty minutes late is normal. Arriving early is the real mistake: the host may still be in the shower.
That's social life only. For work, classes and the doctor, be on time, or at least text. (The doctor may still keep you waiting.)

pages.prompt: Your friend texts **“ya salgo”**: I'm leaving now. What's she most likely doing?
pages.explain: **Ya salgo** always includes some extra time, and **llego en cinco** means fifteen. Nobody's lying: everyone knows how to read it.

pages.text: Plans live in the WhatsApp group, and the key phrase is **vamos viendo**: let's see. The plan is alive, but nothing's fixed until an hour before.
Never show up empty-handed. Ask **“¿Qué llevo?”**, what should I bring? The host will say **“no traigas nada”**, don't bring anything. Bring wine or **helado**, ice cream, anyway.

pages.prompt: You announce **“bueno, me voy yendo”**: well, I'm heading off. How long until you're out the door?
pages.explain: Half an hour, easily. Another glass appears. Then a kiss for everyone. Then a chat at the door. Totally normal.

pages.text: Slipping out without goodbyes is **irse a la francesa**: leaving French-style. People notice, and they'll bring it up next time.

classes.title: Going out
classes.summary: The previa, the boliche and breakfast at sunrise

pages.text: The **boliche**, the nightclub, opens around one. The dancing really starts at two or three. Getting home at six, with the sun up, is a normal Saturday.

pages.prompt: Your friends say: “Previa at Tomi's, then the boliche.” You get to Tomi's at nine. What do you find?
options: The party already in full swing
pages.explain: At nine most people haven't even had dinner. The previa gets going around eleven or midnight.

pages.text: **La previa** is drinks at a friend's place before going out: cheaper, your own music, and you can hear each other. For plenty of people it's the best part. The boliche is just the excuse.

pages.prompt: It's 4 a.m. and the boliche is packed. Which of these will you almost never hear?
pages.explain: Tango lives in the **milongas**, with their own crowd. The boliche runs on reggaetón, cumbia, electronic music and whatever everyone can shout along to.

pages.text: And six a.m. isn't always the end. Some go on to an **after**, a party after the boliche closes. Everyone else heads for **café con medialunas** as the cafés open, then sleeps until lunch.
Not into boliches? Most nights out are simpler: dinner at half past nine or ten, then **un bar** or **una birra**, a beer, with friends. At seven, restaurants are still empty.

classes.title: No filter
classes.summary: Body comments, money talk, and the gauchada

pages.text: Your aunt sees you after the holidays: **“¡Estás más gordito!”** You've put on a bit of weight. She doesn't mean it as an insult. For her generation it's just an observation, like “you got a haircut.”
Couples call each other **gordo** and **gorda** as a pet name, whatever their size. Friends use **flaco** or **negro** the same way, with love. Don't copy them with people you don't know well.

pages.prompt: A stranger on the street shouts **“¡Flaco!”** at you. Skinny! What does he want?
options: To say you look too thin today
To warn you about a pickpocket
pages.explain: **Flaco** is how you call out to a guy you don't know, and **flaca** to a woman. **“¡Flaco, se te cayó esto!”** Hey, you dropped this. You'll also hear **jefe** and **maestro**.

pages.text: Younger people are more careful with body comments. Laugh off grandma's, but don't start making your own.

pages.prompt: Someone you just met at a party asks how much you pay in rent. How should you take it?
options: As a sign she's flat hunting
pages.explain: After decades of inflation, prices are everyone's favorite topic. **¿Cuánto pagaste?**, how much did you pay?, is a normal question for your phone, your shoes, your rent. Asking someone's salary is still not polite.

pages.text: People ask personal questions early: **¿Tenés novio?** Do you have a boyfriend? They interrupt, talk over each other and give opinions on politics and football. It's interest, not rudeness.
Need a hand? Ask **“¿Me hacés una gauchada?”** Can you do me a favor? A **gauchada** is a favor done for free: a ride to the airport, a borrowed drill. Nobody expects anything back.

classes.title: Christmas in summer
classes.summary: Cold vitel toné, fireworks at midnight, then the beach

pages.text: Christmas in Argentina falls in summer. It can be scorching, and Papá Noel still wears his wool coat.

The **arbolito**, the Christmas tree, goes up on **8 December**, a public holiday (**Día de la Virgen**). The big night isn't the 25th: it's **Nochebuena**, the 24th, with a long dinner, often outdoors.

pages.prompt: It's Nochebuena. Which of these is a classic on the table?
options: Veal in a creamy tuna sauce
pages.explain: **Vitel toné**, an Italian import, served cold: in this heat, most of the food is. Plus **pan dulce** (sweet bread with fruit), **turrón** (nougat) and **sidra** (sparkling cider). And yes, often an asado too.

pages.text: At midnight everyone stands for the **brindis**, the toast: **¡Salud!** and **¡Feliz Navidad!** Fireworks go off across the sky, though fewer each year: loud ones are now banned in many places.

pages.prompt: When do most families open the presents?
pages.explain: Presents at midnight, with the fireworks still going. The 25th is for leftovers and naps.

pages.text: New Year's repeats the formula: dinner, toast, fireworks. Then Buenos Aires gets quiet. January is holiday month, and many who can head for the coast.
On 6 January, kids leave their shoes out with grass and water for the camels of the **Reyes Magos**, the Three Kings.

classes.title: The calendar
classes.summary: Friends' Day, spring, long weekends and birthdays

pages.text: On **20 de julio** Argentina celebrates **Día del Amigo**, Friends' Day. Restaurants are packed and your phone won't stop buzzing: **“¡Feliz Día del Amigo!”**

pages.prompt: Why July 20?
options: It's the day humans first walked on the Moon
It's the birthday of a famous tango singer
It's the day Argentina's first club was founded
pages.explain: An Argentine, **Enrique Febbraro**, watched the Moon landing and thought the whole world should celebrate friendship that day.

pages.text: **21 de septiembre** is a double party: first day of spring and **Día del Estudiante**. Students fill the parks with picnics and guitars. Looking for a quiet park? Pick another day.
Argentines love a **finde largo**, a long weekend. Most years the government even adds a **feriado puente** or two: a bridge day off, just to join a holiday to the weekend.
The birthday song here is **“Que los cumplas feliz”**. Then someone may pull your ears: the **tirón de orejas**, one tug for each year. Mostly a thing for kids.

pages.prompt: Your friend's birthday is tomorrow and you won't see her. When do you send your message?
pages.explain: Wishing **feliz cumple** early brings **yeta**: bad luck. Even Pope Francis, a porteño, warned a crowd who greeted him early, before his 80th birthday.

pages.text: Close friends often write right at midnight. Any time on the day is fine. Just not the day before.

classes.title: What to say, and what not to say
classes.summary: Permiso, provecho, Malvinas and a few lines to keep to yourself

pages.text: Walking into someone's home, say **“Permiso”** at the door, even if they just invited you in. It means “with your permission”. The answer is **“Pasá, pasá”**: come in, come in.

pages.prompt: The bondi is packed and the next stop is yours. What do you say to get to the door?
pages.explain: **Permiso** is for before you pass. If you bump into someone, that's **perdón**. Keep **lo siento** for sad news: it means you feel sorry for someone.

pages.text: See someone eating, at the next table or at their desk at work? Say **“Buen provecho”**, or just **“Provecho”**: enjoy your meal. They'll answer **“Gracias”**, often with a full mouth.
Invited to eat at someone's home? Two lines do the job. Before, **“¿Qué llevo?”** What should I bring? After, to the cook, **“Estuvo riquísimo.”** It was delicious.

pages.prompt: At dinner, people start talking about the islands in the South Atlantic that Argentina and Britain fought over in 1982. What do you call them?
pages.explain: Here they are **las Malvinas**, in Spanish and in English. The other name sounds like you're taking a side. It's a painful subject for many families.

pages.text: Friends call each other **negro**, **gordo** or **flaco**. Between them it's affection, and it isn't about skin or weight. Understand it and smile. As a foreigner, don't copy it.
New friends may ask how old you are, if you're married, or why you have no kids. That's warmth, not an interview. Give a short answer and send it back: **“¿Y vos?”**

pages.prompt: You want to say something nice about Argentina. Which of these goes down badly?
options: “It's a lot like Chile and Uruguay.”
pages.explain: Each country is proud of its own accent, food and history, and neighbors are also rivals. Ask what is different here. You'll get a long, happy answer.

pages.text: In Argentina, **América** is the whole continent, from Canada down to Patagonia. For the United States, say **Estados Unidos**.

sections.title: Buenos Aires
sections.summary: Barrios, bondis, cafés and the city that never goes to bed

classes.title: Porteños and everyone else
classes.summary: Capital, Provincia, el interior, and what they say about each other

pages.text: People from the city of Buenos Aires are **porteños**, people of the port. For centuries, ships, goods and millions of immigrants all came in through here.

pages.prompt: Is the city of Buenos Aires part of the Province of Buenos Aires?
options: No, the city is on its own
Only the southern half of it
pages.explain: The city, **CABA**, is its own district. The Provincia wraps around it, and its capital is a different city: **La Plata**.

pages.text: Cross the **General Paz** avenue and you're in the **conurbano**, a huge ring of suburbs where millions more live. People out there aren't porteños, and they call the city just **Capital**.
Porteños call everywhere outside the metro area **el interior**. People from Córdoba or Mendoza don't love it: it makes the whole country sound like a backyard.

pages.prompt: The provinces have a famous saying about this: “God is everywhere…” How does it end?
options: “…but his office is in Buenos Aires”
pages.explain: **“Dios está en todas partes, pero atiende en Buenos Aires.”** Everything important gets decided in the capital, and everyone else has to go and ask.

pages.text: The stereotypes go both ways. The provinces say porteños are **agrandados**, people who think they are better than everyone, and talk too fast. Porteños joke that the provinces live slower. Both sides exaggerate, and both laugh.
Traveling around? Don't say you're touring “el interior”. Name the province: **“Estoy recorriendo Mendoza.”**

classes.title: A city of barrios
classes.summary: La Boca, San Telmo, Palermo and a cemetery full of legends

pages.text: Ask porteños where they're from and you'll get a barrio, not a city: Boedo, Flores, Palermo. Each has its own cafés, its own club and its own pride.
Porteños give an address as two streets that cross: **“Corrientes y Callao”**. Distance is counted in blocks: **“Son cinco cuadras”**, it's five blocks.
**La Boca** sits where the Riachuelo meets the Río de la Plata. Its dockworkers built houses of wood and **chapa** (metal sheets), painted, the story goes, with paint left over from the shipyards.

pages.prompt: La Boca's famous colorful street, **Caminito**, is named after what?
pages.explain: The tango **“Caminito”**, by **Juan de Dios Filiberto**, a composer from La Boca itself.

pages.text: **San Telmo** is the old colonial south: cobblestones, balconies, antique shops. On Sundays, calle **Defensa** turns into a street market, with tango dancers on the corners.

**Palermo** is the biggest barrio, so people keep inventing sub-barrios: **Palermo Soho**, **Palermo Hollywood**, even “Palermo Queens” for the barrio next door. The joke: soon everything will be “Palermo something”.
In the **Recoleta Cemetery**, marble family vaults line the paths like little streets, with presidents, writers and lots of cats. Most visitors come for one grave: **Evita**'s.

pages.prompt: Another famous tomb there belongs to a young woman, Rufina Cambaceres. What's her legend?
pages.explain: The story goes that she woke up inside her coffin. Historians doubt it, but the legend always wins.

classes.title: Bondi, subte, tacho
classes.summary: The bondi, the sacred cola, and a surprisingly old subte

pages.text: The city bus is the **colectivo**, but everyone calls it **bondi**. And porteños invented it.
You can't pay cash on the bondi. Tap a **SUBE** card, sold at kioscos and subte stations. Many lines also take a bank card or phone. Tell the driver where you're going: **“Hasta Plaza Italia.”**

pages.prompt: How was the colectivo born, in 1928?
options: Taxi drivers began sharing their cars
The city bought old buses from London
A tram company swapped rails for trucks
pages.explain: Taxi drivers short on customers charged each passenger a fixed fare along a route. Soon they stretched the cars to fit more seats.

pages.text: The bondi only stops if you ask. When your line comes, stick your arm out, or it drives right past you. To get off, press the **timbre** (the bell) before your stop and leave by the back door.
At the stop, people line up along the wall: **la cola**. It's sacred. Cut it and the whole line will let you know: **“¡Hay cola, eh!”**
Taxis are black and yellow, and a free one shows a red **LIBRE** light. Porteños call the taxi a **tacho** and the driver a **tachero**.

pages.prompt: The **subte**, Buenos Aires' metro, opened in 1913. Which of these is younger?
pages.explain: Madrid's opened in 1919. The subte was the first metro in all of Latin America.

pages.text: On the bondi and not sure where to get off? Ask the driver **“¿Me avisás cuando lleguemos a…?”** Most will call out your stop.

classes.title: Obelisco, Colón and a pink house
classes.summary: A monument almost torn down, a pink palace and a café with no rush

pages.text: The **Obelisco** went up in a rush in 1936, and plenty of porteños hated it.

pages.prompt: A few years later, what did the city council vote to do with it?
pages.explain: They voted to demolish it, and the mayor vetoed the decision. Today it's where the whole city goes to celebrate a World Cup, or to protest.

pages.text: It stands on **Avenida 9 de Julio**, which porteños proudly call the widest avenue in the world. Crossing on foot usually takes more than one green light.
The president's office is the **Casa Rosada**. The popular story: President **Sarmiento** had it painted pink to mix the red and white of two rival parties.
In front of it is the **Plaza de Mayo**, where the country comes to celebrate and to protest. The **Madres de Plaza de Mayo** have walked around it every Thursday since 1977.

pages.prompt: There's a messier theory for the pink. What?
pages.explain: The story goes that the lime paint was mixed with cow's blood, a trick against the damp. Nobody can prove either story, and the red-and-white one is nicer.

pages.text: Singers and conductors rank the **Teatro Colón** among the best opera houses in the world for its sound. The cheapest seats, way up top, are called **el paraíso**: paradise.
At any neighborhood café, order a **cortado** (espresso with a little milk) and stay two hours. Nobody will rush you. The famous one is the **Tortoni**, with a line of tourists at the door.

classes.title: Five things you'll notice in your first week
classes.summary: Therapy talk, dog packs, a street that never sleeps, and ¡ojo!

pages.text: A Soda Stereo song calls Buenos Aires **la ciudad de la furia**, the city of fury. Fast, loud, horns honking. Most of that fury is noise, not danger.

pages.prompt: Buenos Aires has more of one profession per person than almost anywhere. Which?
pages.explain: **Hacer terapia** is no secret here. **“Lo hablo con mi psicóloga”** is a normal thing to say at dinner.

pages.text: In Palermo or Recoleta you'll meet a **paseaperros**, a dog walker, dragged along by a whole pack of dogs at once. The pack gets the sidewalk.
Avenida **Corrientes** is the city's Broadway: theaters, and bookshops open late. People call it **la calle que nunca duerme**, the street that never sleeps.

pages.prompt: On Avenida **Santa Fe**, **El Ateneo Grand Splendid**, often called one of the world's most beautiful bookshops, used to be something else. What?
pages.explain: An old theater, turned bookshop. The café sits right on the old stage.

pages.text: The thief to know is the **motochorro**, who snatches phones from the back of a motorbike. Porteños aren't paranoid, just alert. Keep your phone off café tables by the street.
A word you'll hear a lot in your first week: **¡Ojo!**, literally “eye!”. It means watch out. **“¡Ojo con el celu!”** Careful with your phone.

classes.title: SUBE: one card for everything
classes.summary: Loading it, tapping it, and reading the subte like a local

pages.text: The **SUBE** is one blue card for the bus, the subte and the train. Get one on your first day and keep it in your pocket. You'll tap it several times a day.
The card holds credit, your **saldo**. To add more, go to a kiosco with a SUBE sign and ask **“¿Me cargás la SUBE?”** Can you load my SUBE? Say how much. Subte stations have machines too.

pages.prompt: The bus is here and your SUBE has no credit left. What happens when you tap?
options: It lets you ride and goes a little below zero
It beeps red and you have to get off
The driver sells you a paper ticket
pages.explain: The card can go a little into the red: **saldo negativo**. You pay it back the next time you load. The limit is small, so load it soon.

pages.text: Not sure it's your bus? Ask before you get on: **“¿Este va a Retiro?”** Does this one go to Retiro? Then tell the driver your stop, wait for his nod, and tap. Longer trips cost more.

pages.prompt: Three friends get on a bondi with only one SUBE between them. Can they all ride?
options: Yes, one card can pay for all three
No, each rider needs their own card
Only if the driver knows them
pages.explain: Tell the driver **“Tres, hasta Plaza Italia”** and tap once for each person. Just check you have enough saldo first.

pages.text: Every subte turnstile also takes a contactless bank card or a phone, and more bus lines add this all the time. Not every bus has it yet, so the SUBE is still the safe choice.
The subte has six lines, each with a letter and a color: **A, B, C, D, E** and **H**. To change from one line to another, follow the signs that say **combinación**.

pages.prompt: You're on the platform of the D line. What tells you which way the train is going?
options: The name of the last station on the line
A number on the front of the train
pages.explain: Signs show the end of the line: **“a Catedral”** or **“a Congreso de Tucumán”**. Before you go down, check which end is past your stop.

pages.text: The subte closes at night, but many bondis run until morning. Tired? Take a taxi or an app like Uber, Cabify or DiDi. And on any bus: **“¿Me avisás dónde me bajo?”** Can you tell me where to get off?

classes.title: Paying like a local
classes.summary: QR codes, cuotas, cash discounts and the hunt for small notes

pages.text: Argentines pay for almost everything with their phone. A fruit stand, a taxi, a street musician: each one has a **QR** code, and most people scan it with an app called **Mercado Pago**.

pages.prompt: A friend owes you her half of dinner. She takes out her phone and says **“Pasame tu alias.”** What is she asking for?
options: The short name of your bank account
The nickname your friends call you
pages.explain: An **alias** is a few easy words that stand for an account. With it she can send you the money in seconds: **“Te transfiero.”**

pages.text: Paying by **transferencia**, a bank transfer, is normal even in tiny shops. You send the money, show your screen, and the seller checks it arrived. It needs an Argentine account, so visitors mostly use a card or cash.

Pay by card and you may hear **“¿En cuotas?”** In monthly payments? Locals split big purchases into **cuotas**, and shop windows promise **“12 cuotas sin interés”**. With a foreign card, just say **“en un pago”**: all at once.

pages.prompt: A shop window says **“Descuento en efectivo”**: a discount for cash. Why would a shop want cash that much?
options: Card money arrives later and costs the shop a fee
Cash is quicker to count at closing time
Card machines stop working when it rains
pages.explain: With a card, the shop pays a fee and may wait for its money. When prices keep rising, waiting costs money too. So it's always worth asking: **“¿Hay descuento en efectivo?”**

pages.text: Small shops often have no change. You'll hear **“¿Tenés más chico?”** Do you have a smaller note? Keep your small notes for kioscos and taxis, and break the big ones at the supermarket.

pages.prompt: **“¿Me hacés precio?”** means “Can you give me a better price?” Where can you ask it?
options: At a street market, buying three things
At a restaurant, when the bill comes
pages.explain: It works at a **feria** (a street market), with antiques or crafts, or when you buy several things in a small shop. Ask once, with a smile. Not where the prices are fixed.

pages.text: Visiting? The rules for foreign cards and for changing money have changed many times. Before you travel, check what rate your card gets right now. Bring some cash too, and change it at a bank or a **casa de cambio**.
At a restaurant, the tip is about 10% and people usually leave it in cash on the table, even when they pay the bill by card.

classes.title: Street smarts
classes.summary: Small habits locals have, and what to say if something happens

pages.text: Buenos Aires is a big city, and big-city rules apply. Most visits go by with no trouble at all. Locals just have a few habits they follow without thinking. Copy them and relax.
First habit: the phone. Don't use it at the edge of the sidewalk, next to the traffic. To read a map or answer a message, step into a doorway or a shop.

pages.prompt: The subte is packed at rush hour. Where do many locals carry their backpack?
options: On their back, straps pulled tight
On the floor, between their feet
pages.explain: You'll see half the carriage wearing the **mochila** (backpack) in front, with the zips closed. It's also good manners: it leaves more room for everyone.

pages.scenario: A friendly stranger points at your jacket: something dirty has landed on it. He takes out tissues and offers to help you clean it.
pages.prompt: What do locals do?
options: Stop and let him wipe it off
Put the bag down and clean it
pages.explain: It's an old trick, **la mancha**, the stain. One person makes the stain, another “helps”, and while you're busy, your bag or wallet is gone. Keep walking and clean it later, inside a café.

pages.text: Streets change after dark. An avenue full of people at noon can be empty at midnight. Ask someone at your hotel or a café: **“¿Es tranquilo por acá de noche?”** Is it calm around here at night?
Late at night, don't walk long empty blocks. Order a car with an app, or ask the restaurant to call a **radio taxi**: a taxi booked by phone, so the company knows who is driving you.

pages.prompt: Someone grabs your phone and runs. What do Argentines tell each other to do?
options: Let it go, you matter more than the phone
Run after him and shout for help
Hold on to it as hard as you can
pages.explain: Everyone gives the same advice: don't fight for a thing. A phone can be replaced. Then ask the people around you for help. They usually stop.

pages.text: Three things to say. **“¡Cuidado!”** Careful! **“Me robaron.”** I was robbed. **“¿Me ayudás?”** Can you help me? In Buenos Aires, the emergency number for the police is **911**.
If something is stolen, go to a **comisaría**, a police station, and make a **denuncia**, a report. Your insurance and your embassy will ask for that paper.

classes.title: Ordering at a café
classes.summary: Lágrima, submarino, two kinds of medialunas and a free glass of soda

pages.text: Ask for **un café** and you get a small, strong espresso. There are no sizes to choose and nobody writes your name on a cup. Want a bit more? Ask for it **en jarrito**, in a taller cup.

pages.prompt: The menu lists **una lágrima**: “a tear”. What arrives at your table?
options: Hot milk with a drop of coffee
Coffee with a drop of cold milk
Coffee with a drop of liquor
pages.explain: The “tear” is the coffee: just a drop in a cup of hot milk. It's the softest coffee on the menu.

pages.text: From the most coffee to the most milk: **café**, **cortado**, **café con leche** (about half and half), **lágrima**. A big mug of black filter coffee is hard to find in a classic café.
The classic order is **café con leche con medialunas**, small sweet croissants. There are two kinds: **de manteca** (butter), soft and shiny, and **de grasa** (lard), thinner, crisper and less sweet.

pages.prompt: You order a **submarino**. The waiter brings a tall glass of hot milk and… what?
options: A bar of chocolate to drop in
A small coffee to pour in
A scoop of ice cream on a spoon
pages.explain: You sink the chocolate bar in the milk, like a submarine, and stir until it melts. Kids love it, and so do adults on a cold day.

pages.text: Many cafés bring a tiny glass of **soda**, fizzy water, with your coffee. It's free. For something salty, order a **tostado**: a toasted ham and cheese sandwich on thin white bread.
The waiter is the **mozo**. In a classic café you sit down first and he comes to you. To call him, raise a hand and say **“Disculpá”**. You order and pay at the table.
At a newer café they ask at the counter: **“¿Para acá o para llevar?”** For here or to go? When you want to pay at a table, say **“¿Me cobrás?”** Can you charge me?

sections.title: Cómo hablamos
sections.summary: Vos, the “sh” sound, lunfardo and talking with your hands

classes.title: Vos, not tú
classes.summary: The little pronoun that makes you sound Argentine

pages.text: Your textbook taught you **tú**. Forget it here. Argentines say **vos**: **vos sos**, **vos tenés**, **¿vos querés?** Say “tú tienes” and people understand you, then know at once that you learned from a textbook.
Why vos? It's old Spanish. The usual story: **tú** took over in the rich colonial capitals, Lima and Mexico City. The Río de la Plata was a poor, far-off corner, and nobody updated it.

pages.prompt: So what did Argentine schools teach kids for decades?
options: Tú, which nobody said at home
pages.explain: Grammar books kept pushing **tú**. Only in 1982 did the Academia Argentina de Letras accept vos as correct, educated Spanish.

pages.text: Plural “you” is always **ustedes**. **Vosotros** is for Spain. Here it survives mainly in the national anthem, which opens with **“Oíd, mortales”**.

pages.prompt: In Buenos Aires, who usually gets the formal **usted**?
options: Few people, mostly in formal moments
pages.explain: The waiter, the shop clerk, often even your friend's grandma: **vos**. Usted still shows up with older strangers and in formal settings, and more outside Buenos Aires, but vos is the normal default.

pages.text: So politeness lives in the tone: **disculpá**, **¿me podrías…?**, **por favor**. A warm vos usually beats a stiff usted.
You don't even need to say vos. The ending does the work: **¿Tenés cambio?** is the whole sentence. Short, friendly, local.

classes.title: Sho, che and the melody
classes.summary: The sound, the word and the tune that give a porteño away

pages.text: The quickest way to spot a porteño: **y** and **ll** sound like “sh”. **Yo** is “sho”, **calle** is “cashe”, **me llamo** is “me shamo”.

pages.prompt: A Buenos Aires grandma and her granddaughter both say **yo**. What's different?
options: Nothing: the sound hasn't changed in a century
Grandma says “yo”, just like in Madrid
pages.explain: The older sound is a buzzing **zh**, like the s in *measure*. Younger porteños, led by women, pushed it to a crisp **sh**. Both are 100% porteño.

pages.text: The sh isn't only Argentine, it's **rioplatense**: Montevideo says it too. And not all of Argentina does. Much of the interior, like Córdoba, Cuyo, the north and the northeast, keeps a softer y.

pages.prompt: Researchers compared the melody of Buenos Aires Spanish with other ways of speaking. Which was it closest to?
pages.explain: Researchers at CONICET, Argentina's science agency, found it closer to **Naples** than to Madrid. That's why foreigners say porteños sound a bit Italian.

pages.text: The tune most likely arrived with the Italian immigrants around 1900. Their accents faded, but the melody stuck.
Then there's **che**: hey, dude, listen. Nobody knows for sure where it comes from. An old Spanish call for attention, **ce**? Guaraní? Mapudungun? Valencian? Pick a theory and defend it over a mate.

pages.prompt: Ernesto Guevara became world-famous as “Che”. Who gave him the nickname?
options: His Cuban comrades, because he said it constantly
His mother, who called him that as a baby
The press, after his first speech in Havana
pages.explain: To the Cubans, **che** was the most Argentine thing about him. It became his name.

pages.text: End a story with **¿viste?**, “you know?”, and you'll sound local instantly: **Hacía un frío, ¿viste?**

classes.title: Lunfardo
classes.summary: The street slang born in the conventillos

pages.text: Around 1900, Buenos Aires was packed with immigrants, mostly Italians and Spaniards, crammed into tenements called **conventillos**. Out of that mix came **lunfardo**, the city's street slang.

pages.prompt: Who were the first people to write lunfardo down, in the late 1800s?
options: Police, who thought it was a thieves' code
Teachers, trying to stamp it out
pages.explain: Police officers and criminologists. Then it turned out bakers, clerks and grandmas talked like that too.

pages.text: Then **tango** carried it onto the radio, and lunfardo went from the tenement patio to every living room in the country.
It's no museum piece. Everyone, from teenagers to bank managers, says **me voy al laburo**, I'm off to work. It comes from the Italian of the immigrants: *lavoro*, work.
More lunfardo you'll hear every day: **guita**, money. **Pibe** and **piba**, a boy and a girl. **Morfar**, to eat. **Birra**, beer. **Fiaca**, the feeling of not wanting to do anything.

pages.prompt: The city bus is the **bondi**. According to the usual story, where does the word come from?
options: The name of an Italian bus company
A Guaraní word for a big box
pages.explain: Brazilians called trams **bonde**, supposedly after the bonds sold as tickets. Buenos Aires borrowed it, and when the trams vanished, the name jumped onto the bus.

pages.text: **Chamuyo** is smooth talk: half truth, all charm. You can **chamuyar** a date, a cop, your boss. And when a story sounds too good: **eso es puro chamuyo**.
One to hear, not say: **mina**, for a woman. Many people use it, women too, but it can sound macho, and from a foreigner it can sound rude.
Slang has its own academy here: the **Academia Porteña del Lunfardo**, founded in 1962. Scholars meet to study street words the way others study Cervantes.

classes.title: Vesre, re and posta
classes.summary: Words backwards, words turned up, and the truth

pages.text: Porteños love flipping words. Swap the syllables of **revés**, backwards, and you get **vesre**: the name of the game, played on itself.

pages.prompt: Flipped words sound like a party game, but one of these is completely everyday. Which?
pages.explain: **¿Quién garpa?**, who's paying?, ends plenty of dinners. **Gotán** and **dorima** mostly live in old tangos.

pages.text: Another flip you'll hear constantly: **hotel** becomes **telo**. Remember that one. It matters.

pages.prompt: At a party you say you're staying at “un telo re lindo en Palermo”. Everyone bursts out laughing. Why?
options: A telo is a hotel rented by the hour
Telo is slang for a cheap hostel
Telo is what little kids call a hotel
pages.explain: A **telo** is a love hotel: rooms by the hour, discreet entrance. Great story for the rest of the night, though.

pages.text: Plenty of people live with their parents well into their twenties, so telos are a normal part of city life, used by couples of all ages. For your stay, just say **hotel**.
Want “very”? Put **re** in front: **re lindo**, **re lejos**. It even works alone: **—¿Te gustó? —¡Re!**
**Posta** means “for real”. **¿Posta?** is “Seriously?”, and **la posta** is the real story. Now you know why this app is called Posta.

classes.title: Hands and texts
classes.summary: Gestures you'll see and shortcuts you'll read

pages.text: Porteños don't just talk, they perform. Watch two friends argue about football across the street and you'll get the gist without hearing a word.

pages.prompt: Someone cuts in the bus line. A lady pinches her fingertips together, pointing up, and bobs her wrist. What's she saying?
pages.explain: That's the **montoncito**: **¿qué te pasa?** From friendly to threatening, depending on the face. It even has its own emoji: 🤌.

pages.text: Two more you'll see daily. Flat hand rocking side to side: **más o menos**. Finger pulling down your lower eyelid: careful, **¡ojo!**

pages.prompt: You ask a man where the bus stops. He brushes the back of his fingers forward from under his chin. What is he telling you?
pages.explain: It means **ni idea**, no idea. In Italy the same move means “I don't care”, but here it isn't rude.

pages.text: Argentines love **audios**: WhatsApp voice notes instead of typing. A three-minute audio just to say you're running late? Completely normal.
When they do type, they cut words short: **q** is que, **xq** is porque, **tmb** is también, **dsp** is después. And **tqm**, te quiero mucho, closes many family chats.

pages.prompt: You suggest a 7 a.m. Sunday run. Your friend replies: **“bue”**. How excited are they?
pages.explain: **Bue** is **bueno** with a sigh: fine, if we must. Stretched out, **bueee**, it means “oh, come on”.

pages.text: **Dale** is the reply to almost everything: OK, sure, come on, go ahead. **—¿Vamos a las 8? —Dale.** In a chat, it often closes the conversation.

sections.title: La mesa argentina
sections.summary: Empanadas, pizza, milanesas, and dinner at ten

classes.title: Dinner at ten
classes.summary: Late dinners, the merienda, and a bill that never comes

pages.text: Argentines eat late. Breakfast is small and sweet, lunch is around one, dinner around **ten**. Book a restaurant for eight and you'll have the waiters all to yourself.
What gets everyone through? The **merienda**: around five, a small meal of mate or coffee with toast or **facturas**. Skip it and you'll be starving by eight.

pages.prompt: A friend texts: **“Che, ¿venís a tomar unos mates?”** What should you expect?
options: A full merienda and a long chat
Only mate, and nothing to eat
pages.explain: It's an invitation to the merienda: mate, something sweet, and time to talk. The verb is **merendar**: **“¿Merendamos?”** Some older people say **tomar el té**, even with no tea on the table.

pages.text: Kids keep the same hours. At eleven at night you still see families in restaurants, above all on weekends, with little ones running between the tables or asleep across two chairs.

pages.prompt: You finished eating an hour ago. Why hasn't the waiter brought the bill?
options: Bringing it unasked would be like kicking you out
Bills only come once the kitchen has closed
He's waiting for you to order a coffee first
pages.explain: The table is yours until you ask: **“¿Me traés la cuenta?”** Or catch the **mozo**'s eye and pretend to write in the air.

pages.text: The reason is the **sobremesa**: the long chat after the meal, over coffee. It often lasts longer than the meal itself, and nobody rushes you.
The tip, **la propina**, is about 10%, usually left in cash. It is not on the bill. The **cubierto** you see there is a table charge, not the tip.

pages.prompt: Six friends, one bill. You only had a salad, Tomi had the steak. How does the table usually pay?
options: Each person pays for their own dish
pages.explain: Among friends, the bill usually gets split evenly. If the gap is big, someone may offer to split it by what each person had.

pages.text: To split the bill evenly, say **“¿Dividimos?”** Putting money together to buy something, like the meat for an asado or a gift, is **hacer una vaquita**.

classes.title: Empanadas
classes.summary: A secret code in the fold, and a war between provinces

pages.text: Party for twenty or a lazy Sunday night, the answer is the same: **empanadas**, ordered by the **docena**, the dozen. Half-moons of dough, baked or fried, a different filling in each.

pages.prompt: A dozen empanadas arrive: four fillings, nothing written on them. How do you tell them apart?
options: By the pattern folded into the edge
By a little dot of color on top
By a number stamped into the dough
pages.explain: The braided edge, the **repulgue**, is a code. Each filling gets its own fold.

pages.text: There's no national code, though. Every shop and every grandma has her own system. If it's not on the box, just ask: **“¿Cuál es cuál?”**

The usual fillings: **carne** (beef, **suave** or **picante**), **pollo** (chicken), **jamón y queso**, **humita** (corn) and **verdura** (greens). To order: **“Una docena: seis de carne, tres de pollo y tres de humita.”**
The northwest takes this very seriously. **Salta** and **Tucumán** each claim the best empanada in the country, and neither will ever back down.

pages.prompt: What is one famous difference between a salteña and a tucumana?
pages.explain: Salteñas get little cubes of **papa**. Put potato in a tucumana and someone from Tucumán will explain your mistake for twenty minutes.

pages.text: On good menus you'll see **cortada a cuchillo**: beef chopped by hand, not ground. It keeps the filling juicy.
A good empanada is full of hot juice. Locals say you eat it **con las piernas abiertas**, legs apart, so the juice misses your pants. In Tucumán, many add a squeeze of lemon before each bite.

classes.title: Pizza porteña
classes.summary: Thick, cheesy, eaten standing up, with fainá on top

pages.text: Buenos Aires pizza is its own thing. The classic is thick, fluffy dough under a huge amount of cheese. The default order is a **muzza**: tomato, cheese, a few green olives.
You choose the dough: **al molde** is the thick classic, **a la piedra** is thin and crisp, **media masa** is in between. Order **“una grande de muzza”**, or just **“dos porciones”**, two slices.
Then there's the **fugazzeta**: a mountain of onion over cheese. Order it **rellena** and the cheese comes inside the dough too. Careful: a **fugazza** is onion only, no cheese.

pages.prompt: Porteños often put something on top of their slice of pizza. What is it?
pages.explain: It's **fainá**, a chickpea flatbread brought by Genoese immigrants. Pizza with fainá on top is pizza **a caballo**: on horseback.

pages.text: Add a glass of cheap, sweet **moscato** and you've got the old porteño trio: **moscato, pizza y fainá**.
**Avenida Corrientes**, the theater street, is also the pizza street. The famous pizzerías there stay packed until long after the last show.

pages.prompt: The play just ended and the pizzería is packed. What do porteños do?
options: Eat a slice standing at the counter
Take a number and wait an hour
Buy a pizza to eat in the theater
pages.explain: Eating **de parado** at the counter, a **porción** in your hand, is a classic. Faster, cheaper, and honestly more fun.

classes.title: Nona's kitchen
classes.summary: Milanesas, Sunday pasta and ñoquis on the 29th

pages.text: Italian cooking came with the immigrants and became the national kitchen. In many families, grandma and grandpa are still **la nona** and **el nono**.

The home-cooked star is the **milanesa**, or just **mila**: thin beef or chicken, breaded and fried or baked. Kids ask for it on their birthday, and the leftovers become tomorrow's **sánguche de milanesa**.

pages.prompt: The **milanesa a la napolitana** comes with ham, cheese and tomato sauce. Where was it born?
pages.explain: At a restaurant called **Nápoli**, near the Luna Park stadium. The story goes a cook burnt a milanesa and hid the damage under ham, cheese and sauce.

pages.text: Sunday lunch at the grandparents' often means homemade pasta with **tuco**, a tomato sauce that simmers all morning. Nobody leaves before the second helping.
On the **29th** of every month, many families eat **ñoquis**. The ritual: a banknote under your plate while you eat, for money and luck.

pages.prompt: Why the 29th? Pick the practical explanation.
options: By then the salary was gone, and gnocchi are cheap
Pasta factories gave away leftovers that day
Italian immigrants got their papers that day
pages.explain: That's the practical explanation: potatoes and flour, the cheapest dinner before payday. There's also an Italian legend: a poor family fed San Pantaleón, and later found gold coins under their plates. Many keep the banknote in their wallet until next month.

pages.text: So a **ñoqui** is also someone with a public job who never works and only shows up at the end of the month, to get paid. It is an insult.

classes.title: Stews and corn
classes.summary: Winter pots, patriotic locro and corn in its husk

pages.text: When winter hits, Argentines go for a **guiso**, a hearty home stew. One pot, cheap cuts, whatever's in the fridge. The everyday classic is **guiso de lentejas**, lentil stew.
The king of them all is **locro**: white corn, beans, squash and several meats, cooked for hours until it's thick.

pages.prompt: When do whole neighborhoods cook giant pots of locro?
options: On national holidays like 25 de mayo
On the first frost of every winter
At the end of the corn harvest
pages.explain: Locro is the patriotic dish on **25 de mayo** (the revolution of 1810) and **9 de julio** (independence, 1816). Many also cook it on May 1st.

pages.text: Clubs, parishes and neighbors cook it in pots big enough to bathe in and sell it by the portion. Bring your own **tupper**, and come early.
Locro is no immigrant dish. It comes from the Andes, from long before Argentina existed. On the side comes a spicy red sauce of oil, paprika and green onion. Ask: **“¿Tenés picante?”**
The **carbonada** is beef, squash, corn and sweet potato, often with dried peaches. The showstopper version is served inside a whole baked pumpkin.

pages.prompt: From the northwest comes **humita en chala**, a fresh corn paste. What is it wrapped in?
pages.explain: Fresh corn grated into a paste, wrapped in the **chala**, the husk, tied up and boiled. You unwrap it at the table like a present.

classes.title: Helado
classes.summary: Italian roots, flavors called gustos, and ice cream by the kilo

pages.text: **Helado** here has Italian roots, and Argentines will tell you it's the best outside Italy. Every neighborhood has a **heladería**, open late, and people eat helado even in winter.
Flavors are called **gustos**, and even the smallest cup gets two. Choosing them is serious business.
At the shop, you usually pay first at the **caja**, then take your ticket to the counter. You can ask to taste: **“¿Puedo probar?”** Then order: **“Un cuarto de dulce de leche granizado y limón.”**

pages.prompt: Winter, 11 p.m., dinner at a friend's place is over. What does the host order?
options: Coffee and cake from a café
pages.explain: Helado comes to your door in a foam tub: **un cuarto** (250 g), **medio kilo** or **un kilo**. Any night, any season.

pages.text: A kilo takes up to four gustos, and it's gone before anyone mentions dieting. **Un cuarto** is for one person with self-control.
A heladería lives or dies by its **dulce de leche**, and the best ones offer it in several versions. With chocolate flakes, it's **dulce de leche granizado**.

pages.prompt: **Sambayón**, a classic flavor, has a surprising ingredient. What is it?
pages.explain: It's the Italian *zabaione*: egg yolks, sugar and sweet wine. A grown-up flavor.

pages.text: Order a dulce de leche, a sambayón, and one fruit flavor so you can say you ate something healthy.

sections.title: Alfajores y dulces
sections.summary: Dulce de leche, facturas and what to buy at the kiosco

classes.title: Dulce de leche and friends
classes.summary: The spread on everything, and the sweets it hangs out with

pages.text: **Dulce de leche** is milk and sugar cooked slowly for hours until thick and brown. On toast, in cakes, straight from the jar with a spoon at midnight.
Just don't call it caramel. Caramel is cooked sugar. Dulce de leche is mostly milk, and Argentines will correct you.

pages.prompt: Legend says dulce de leche was invented by accident in 1829. How?
options: A maid forgot the milk on the stove
A soldier left sugar in his canteen
A baker burned a batch of flan
pages.explain: The story goes: a ranch in Cañuelas, the future governor Rosas meeting his rival Lavalle to sign a truce, and a maid so caught up in the drama she forgot the pot.

pages.text: Cute story, almost certainly a legend. Uruguay, Chile, France and others claim dulce de leche too. Uruguay, loudly.
At the supermarket, **clásico** is soft, for toast and the spoon. **Repostero** is firmer, for baking: it holds its shape inside alfajores without dripping.

pages.prompt: The **chocotorta** is the classic birthday cake. How long does it spend in the oven?
pages.explain: Zero. Chocolinas cookies dipped in milk or coffee, layered with dulce de leche mixed with cream cheese. Into the fridge, done.

pages.text: Two more to know: **pastafrola**, a lattice tart filled with quince or sweet potato paste, and **Mantecol**, a crumbly peanut sweet, a bit like halva, that is on the table every Christmas.

classes.title: What is an alfajor?
classes.summary: Two cookies, dulce de leche in the middle, and a very long trip

pages.text: An **alfajor** is two soft cookies stuck together with a filling, usually dulce de leche, often dipped in chocolate. That's all it is, and the whole country loves it.

pages.prompt: Where do the alfajor's name and ancestor come from?
pages.explain: The name comes from Andalusian Arabic. In al-Ándalus it was a honey, almond and spice sweet, and Andalucía still makes it today. The cookie sandwich came later, in the Americas.

pages.text: The Spanish brought the name across the ocean, and here it became cookies plus dulce de leche. Argentina just, humbly, perfected it.
Every region has its own. **De maicena** is the one your abuela makes: crumbly cornstarch cookies, dulce de leche, edges rolled in grated coconut.
**Marplatense**: dipped in chocolate, the kiosco classic. **Santafesino**: crunchy layers, white sugar glaze. **Cordobés**: soft, glazed, often filled with fruit jam.

pages.prompt: Industry estimates count how many alfajores Argentines eat. How many a day?
pages.explain: Estimates start at about six million a day, and some recent ones are much higher. That's at least one for every eight people, every single day.

pages.text: Skipped lunch? Ask for a **triple**: three cookies, two layers of dulce de leche. More alfajor per alfajor.

classes.title: Brands, kioscos and the eternal debate
classes.summary: Havanna or Jorgito? Pick a side at the kiosco on the corner

pages.text: Every block has a **kiosco**: a tiny shop selling candy, drinks, phone credit and, above all, alfajores. Many stay open late, some never close: look for **24 hs**.

pages.prompt: For years, kioscos often had no coins for your change. What did you get instead?
options: A note saying they owe you
pages.explain: During years of coin shortages, **caramelos** became the unofficial small change. Today coins are almost gone, and most people pay with a QR code or a card.

pages.text: Late at night, many kioscos serve through a small window or a grille, **la reja**. Ask, pay, done.
To buy one, say **“¿Me das un alfajor?”** To ask the price: **“¿Cuánto sale?”** You may get a question back: **“¿Negro o blanco?”**, dark or white chocolate.

pages.prompt: You're meeting your partner's family for the first time. Which alfajores do you bring?
pages.explain: **Havanna**, from Mar del Plata, is the expensive one: the box you bring as a gift.

pages.text: **Jorgito** and **Guaymallén** are the everyday kiosco alfajores: cheap and much loved. Ask a table which alfajor is the best and the argument can last all afternoon.
There's even a **Mundial del Alfajor**, held in Buenos Aires. A “world” championship for a snack that almost only Argentina eats. Very Argentine.

classes.title: Facturas: anarchy at the bakery
classes.summary: Medialunas, bolas de fraile and the rebel bakers who named them

pages.text: **Facturas** are the sweet pastries from the **panadería**, bought by the dozen and wrapped in paper. Everyone mixes their own dozen, and everyone has a favorite.
You choose one by one, pointing. Or say **“una docena surtida”**, a mixed dozen, or **“media docena”**, half a dozen. In a busy bakery, take a number at the door first.

pages.prompt: The queen is the **medialuna**, a small croissant. There are two kinds. How do you tell them apart at a glance?
options: Butter ones are plump and shiny
Butter ones are straight, not curved
Fat ones have sesame on top
pages.explain: **De manteca**, with butter: plump, soft and shiny with syrup. **De grasa**, with beef fat: thinner, flakier, no shine.

pages.text: **De manteca** is the sweet one. **De grasa** is drier and a little salty. Which is better is a national debate.

pages.prompt: Pastries here have names like “friar's balls”, “sacraments” and “little cannons”. Who named them, the story goes?
pages.explain: In 1887 Buenos Aires bakers, many of them Italian and Spanish anarchists, founded their first union. The story goes that during a strike in 1888 they named pastries to mock the Church, the army and the police.

pages.text: The **vigilante**, the cop, is long like a police baton. **Bolas de fraile** and **sacramentos** tease the Church. **Cañoncitos**, little cannons, go after the army.
Historians debate how much of this story is documented. But it's the one every baker will tell you.
Going to a friend's for mate in the afternoon? Stop at the panadería for **una docena de facturas**. Nobody has ever said no.

classes.title: ¿Qué hay de postre?
classes.summary: Flan mixto, a cop's dessert and the other homemade classics

pages.text: Sunday lunch is over and someone asks the big one: **¿qué hay de postre?** At home or at a **bodegón**, an old-school restaurant, the answer is a homemade classic.
**Flan** is egg custard with caramel. Here it rarely comes alone: with dulce de leche, with whipped cream, or both. Both is **mixto**: **“Un flan mixto, por favor.”**

pages.prompt: The bodegón menu offers **postre vigilante**. What arrives?
options: The long pastry from the bakery
Ice cream with dulce de leche
pages.explain: Also called **queso y dulce**: a slice of cheese with quince or sweet potato paste. The story goes police from a station in Palermo ordered it in the 1920s: cheap, quick, and easy to eat with one hand.

pages.text: **Budín de pan** is bread pudding made from yesterday's bread, milk, eggs and caramel. Immigrant thrift turned into dessert.
**Arroz con leche** is rice slowly cooked in milk with sugar, lemon peel and cinnamon. It's also the name of a song every kid knows.

pages.prompt: What's the kids' song **“Arroz con leche”** actually about?
options: A kid sent to buy milk
pages.explain: **“Arroz con leche, me quiero casar…”**: rice pudding, I want to get married. It's a circle game. The pudding just opens the song.

pages.text: **Panqueques** here are thin crêpes rolled around dulce de leche. Some parrillas serve them **quemados**, with the sugar burnt crunchy on top.
Too full for your host's flan? Say **“un poquito nomás”**, just a little bit. Saying no is not an option.

sections.title: Mate
sections.summary: Yerba, the gourd and the rules of sharing it

classes.title: What is mate?
classes.summary: A bitter leaf, a gourd and an invitation

pages.text: **Mate** is hot water poured over **yerba**, dried and ground leaves. You sip it from a small gourd through a metal straw, then it gets refilled and passed on.

pages.prompt: Yerba looks a lot like green tea. Is it the same plant?
options: Yes, it's a tea bush, just dried differently
No, it's a different plant native to South America
pages.explain: A totally different plant from tea, but it does have caffeine. That's why so many people start the day with it.

pages.text: The gourd is also called a **mate**. And the verb is **tomar**, not beber: **¿Tomamos unos mates?** Shall we have some mate?
The **Guaraní** drank yerba long before the Spanish arrived. Later, **Jesuit** missions tamed the wild plant and grew it on plantations.

pages.prompt: In 1767 the Jesuits were expelled. What happened to their yerba plantations?
options: Nobody managed to farm yerba for over a century
Spain took them over and got rich
They moved the plants to Brazil
pages.explain: The way to sprout the seeds was lost. Yerba was picked wild again until around 1900, when growers learned how to do it once more. Most still comes from **Misiones** and **Corrientes**.

pages.text: By law, since 2013, mate is Argentina's **infusión nacional**: the national infusion. (Wine has the title of national drink.) Not bad for a leaf you share with total strangers.
Someone holds up a gourd and asks **¿Querés un mate?** Say **dale**, sure. You just joined the round. And **¿Tomamos unos mates?** often just means: come over and talk.

classes.title: The gear
classes.summary: Gourd, bombilla, termo and yerba: your starter kit

pages.text: The kit: a **mate** (the gourd), a **bombilla** (a metal straw with a filter at the bottom), a **termo** of hot water, and a pack of **yerba**.
The classic mate is a dried gourd, but there are wooden, glass and steel ones too. The big one with a wide mouth, wrapped in leather, is the **mate camionero**: the trucker's mate.

pages.prompt: You just bought a beautiful new gourd. What do you do before your first mate?
options: Fill it with wet yerba and wait a day
Scrub it well with hot soapy water
Leave it out in the sun for a week
pages.explain: That's **curar el mate**, curing it. Only gourd and wooden mates need it. And never use soap: the gourd soaks it up, and so does your next mate.

pages.text: The bombilla goes in once and stays put. It's not a spoon, and never, ever a stirring stick.
Argentine termos come with a special spout, the **pico cebador**. It pours a thin, steady stream right next to the bombilla, without flooding the yerba.

pages.prompt: You open a pack of yerba and it's full of little sticks. Good or bad?
pages.explain: That's **yerba con palo**, the usual kind in Argentina: milder, and it lasts more rounds. **Sin palo**, just leaves, is stronger. First time? Buy con palo.

pages.text: Pick your yerba brand carefully. People are fiercely loyal to theirs, and they'll happily tell you why yours is wrong.

classes.title: How to cebar
classes.summary: The montañita, the right water and the fool's first mate

pages.text: **Cebar** is to pour the water and serve each mate. The person doing it is the **cebador**. **¿Quién ceba?** means: who's serving? A bad cebador hears about it all afternoon.
Fill the gourd about ¾ with yerba. Cover it, flip it, shake, then tilt it. The yerba settles into a slope: the **montañita**, the little mountain.

pages.prompt: How hot should the water be?
pages.explain: Boiling water **quema la yerba**: it burns it, and the mate turns harsh and bitter. Take the **pava**, the kettle, off the heat before it boils. Many electric kettles in Argentina even have a “mate” setting.

pages.text: Pour into the low side, next to the bombilla, and keep the top of the montañita dry. Some cebadores do it differently, and that works too.

pages.prompt: Who usually drinks the very first mate?
pages.explain: The first one is bitter, foamy and full of dust. The cebador drinks it so nobody else has to.

pages.text: It even has a name: **el mate del zonzo**, the fool's mate. A small sacrifice, not a privilege.
After many rounds the flavor fades and the mate is **lavado**: washed out. Time for fresh yerba.

classes.title: The rules of the ronda
classes.summary: Mate etiquette, so you don't get it wrong

pages.text: One mate, one bombilla, one **ronda**. The cebador fills it and hands it to you. You drink all of it, until it gurgles.

pages.prompt: You finish your mate. Who do you hand it to?
pages.explain: Always back to the cebador, who refills it for the next person. The mate never skips the cebador.

pages.text: Only the cebador touches the yerba and the bombilla. Fixing someone's mate is like rearranging their kitchen while they cook.

pages.prompt: You hand the mate back and say **“gracias”**. What happens next?
options: You get the next one first
pages.explain: In a ronda, **gracias** means “I'm done”. Want more? Just hand it back, maybe with a **¡qué rico!**

pages.text: Don't hold the mate while you tell a long story. Everyone's waiting and the water's getting cold. Someone will say **“¡No es un micrófono!”**
Don't wipe the bombilla before you drink. Sharing it is the whole point, and wiping it reads as “you think I'm dirty”.

Got a cold? Don't share: say **“paso, estoy resfriado”** (or **resfriada**). Just don't feel like it? Say **“no, gracias”** the first time it comes your way. Nobody minds. Since the pandemic, many people bring their own mate too.

classes.title: Mate every day
classes.summary: Sweet or bitter, cold or in a cup, everywhere you go

pages.text: Most people drink it **amargo**: bitter, no sugar. **Mate dulce** has sugar, and it's more common in some families and provinces. Purists will tease you. Lovingly.
Old folklore says a mate could carry a message: sweet meant friendship, very hot meant passion, bitter meant indifference. Today bitter just means bitter: it's how most people drink it.
**Mate cocido** is the simple version: yerba in a tea bag, in a regular cup, often with milk. The drink of school breakfasts and the afternoon **merienda**.

pages.prompt: On a road trip, who makes the mate?
pages.explain: The co-pilot is the cebador. Keep them coming, and don't burn the driver.

pages.text: Mate goes everywhere: the office, university, the park, the beach. **Matear** is to drink mate together, and the **matera** is the bag that carries the kit.

pages.prompt: In the northeast, in 40 °C heat, what do many people drink instead of hot mate?
options: Mate with ice-cold water or juice
Hot mate anyway, no matter what
pages.explain: That's **tereré**: cold water or juice, ice and herbs. Huge in Paraguay and in hot provinces like Corrientes, Misiones, Chaco and Formosa.

pages.text: In Buenos Aires, though, hot mate never takes a vacation. Even at the beach in January, someone has the termo.

classes.title: Mate next door
classes.summary: Uruguay, southern Brazil and a surprise buyer far away

pages.text: Argentina doesn't own mate. **Uruguay**, **Paraguay** and southern **Brazil** drink it every day too, and each has its own way of doing it.

pages.prompt: By most counts, which country drinks the most mate per person?
pages.explain: Uruguay, even more than Argentina. In Montevideo people carry the **termo bajo el brazo**, under the arm: to work, to the beach, along the rambla.

pages.text: The twist: Uruguay grows almost no yerba. Most of it comes from **Brazil**, ground fine, almost without stems. Stronger and more bitter.
In southern Brazil, the gaúchos drink **chimarrão**: bright green, powder-fine yerba in a big gourd called a **cuia**. Same ronda, different accent.

pages.prompt: Which country buys the most yerba from Argentina?
pages.explain: Syria, year after year, by a long way. Uruguay buys mostly from Brazil.

pages.text: The link is people. Around 1900 many Syrians and Lebanese moved to Argentina, and some went back home and took mate with them. Today the **Druze** of Syria and Lebanon especially love it.

sections.title: Asado
sections.summary: Fire, meat and a whole Sunday with your people

classes.title: More than a barbecue
classes.summary: Why an asado is a whole afternoon, not a meal

pages.text: An **asado** is grilled meat, sure. But mostly it's an excuse to spend the whole day together. **¿Hacemos un asado?** really means: want to hang out?

pages.prompt: The invite says **“Vení a la una.”** Come at one. When will you probably eat?
pages.explain: The fire is slow, and so is everything else. Have a drink by the grill and eat when the asador says so.

pages.text: Every asado has one **asador**, also called the **parrillero**, in charge of the fire and the meat. It's a role with a lot of pride. Everyone else keeps them company by the grill, drink in hand.
An asado is also how Argentines celebrate almost anything: a birthday, a win, a new job, a Friday.

pages.prompt: Builders just poured the concrete roof of a new house. What does the owner traditionally pay for?
options: An asado for the whole crew
A day off for the whole crew
A cash bonus for the foreman
pages.explain: The **asado de la losa**, for the finished roof slab. The crew grills right there on site, on bricks and a scrap of iron grate.

pages.text: For lots of families it's a weekly date: **el asado del domingo**. Same backyard, same asador, same people.
**Asado** is also the name of a cut: the ribs. So yes, you can eat asado at an asado.

classes.title: Playing with fire
classes.summary: Embers, firewood, salt and how you like it

pages.text: The **parrilla** is the grill: an iron grate, often built into the backyard in brick. A **parrilla** is also a steakhouse: **vamos a una parrilla** means let's go eat grilled meat.
A **quincho** is a roofed space with a parrilla and a long table: in the backyard of a house, or shared on the roof of an apartment building, where neighbors book it for the weekend.

pages.prompt: What's the secret of a good asado fire?
options: No flames under the meat at all
Tall flames, for a crispy outside
A lid on top, to trap the smoke
pages.explain: You cook over **brasas**, embers. The asador burns wood off to one side and shovels embers under the grill, little by little. Flames burn the outside and leave the inside raw.

pages.text: **Leña**, firewood, takes longer, but many swear it tastes better. **Carbón**, charcoal, is faster, so most city asados use it. Ask two Argentines which is best: three opinions.

pages.prompt: What does the asador put on the meat before it hits the grill?
pages.explain: Usually just coarse salt: **sal gruesa** or **sal parrillera**. Good meat and good embers do the rest. Chimichurri waits at the table.

pages.text: Then patience. The big cuts cook slowly, often for an hour and a half or more, and a good asador flips each one only once.
At a restaurant they ask **¿Qué punto?** **Jugoso** is rare to medium-rare, **a punto** is medium, **bien cocido** is well done. Tip: a punto here is often more cooked than you expect.

classes.title: What comes off the grill, and when
classes.summary: Picada, sausages, achuras, then the big cuts

pages.text: While the fire gets ready, there's a **picada**: cheese, **salame**, olives, bread. That way nobody gets too hungry. Don't fill up, though. There's a long way to go.

pages.prompt: How much meat does the host buy per person?
pages.explain: Half a kilo each is the classic rule, bones included. Nobody wants to be the host who ran out.

pages.text: First off the grill: **chorizo** and **morcilla**. They get cut up on a board and passed around, often on a piece of bread.

pages.prompt: The morcilla is dark, soft and rich. What's it made with?
pages.explain: It's blood sausage: soft, mild and a little sweet. Try it on bread. Saying **no, gracias** is fine too.

pages.text: Then the **achuras**, the organ meats: **chinchulines**, crispy grilled intestines, and **mollejas**, sweetbreads, crispy outside and creamy inside. Try the mollejas with lemon.
Finally the main event: **asado de tira** (short ribs), **vacío** (flank) and **entraña** (skirt steak). The asador decides the order. Your job: eat, and say **¡qué rico!**

On the side: bread and **ensalada mixta** (lettuce, tomato, onion), maybe **papas fritas**. Vegetarian? Say **soy vegetariano** (or **vegetariana**) early. There's **provoleta** (grilled cheese), grilled **morrones** (bell peppers) and other vegetables.

classes.title: Choripán, provoleta and the sauces
classes.summary: The sandwich, the grilled cheese and what goes on top

pages.text: **Choripán**: a grilled chorizo split open in a crusty roll. That's it, and it's perfect. Everyone calls it **chori**.
Ask for it **mariposa**, butterfly: the chorizo is split lengthwise and opened flat, so it cooks faster and gets crispy.

pages.prompt: It's 6 a.m. and the boliche just closed. Where's a classic place to get a chori?
options: A food stall by the river
pages.explain: The **carritos de la Costanera**, grill stalls along the river that stay open very late. Smoke, a line, and chimichurri dripping everywhere.

pages.text: Chori is street food everywhere: outside football stadiums, at every festival, and at political rallies.

pages.prompt: Opponents sometimes call rally crowds, mostly Peronist ones, **choripaneros**. What's the insult?
options: They only came for a free chori
The rally was held at a parrilla
pages.explain: The insult says people were brought in with a free sandwich, not real conviction. It's a political insult. Good to understand, better not to say.

pages.text: **Provoleta** is a thick round of provolone-style cheese, grilled crispy outside and melty inside, with oregano and **ají molido**, mild chili flakes. Eat it fast, before it turns to rubber.
Two sauces are always on the table. **Chimichurri**: parsley, oregano, garlic, **ají molido**, vinegar and oil. Not spicy. **Salsa criolla** is tomato, onion and bell pepper.

classes.title: You're invited. Now what?
classes.summary: What to bring, how not to annoy the asador, and the applause

pages.text: Invited? Ask **¿Qué llevo?** What should I bring? Often the answer is drinks or **hielo**, ice. The host usually buys the meat, or friends split the cost later: **después dividimos**.

pages.prompt: Before anything reaches the table, who gets the first bites?
options: The host's parents, out of respect
pages.explain: Hang out by the grill and the asador will pass you a slice of chorizo or molleja on bread, straight off the fire. Stay close and you get to taste first.

pages.text: Golden rule: don't tell the asador how to cook. Not “it needs more heat”, not “in my country we…”. And never touch the tongs.
Want to help? Ask **“¿Te ayudo en algo?”** and do exactly what you're told. Or just bring the asador a glass of wine.

pages.prompt: The meat reaches the table and everyone starts eating. What does someone always call out?
options: A round of applause for the asador
A short speech from the host
A group photo for the family chat
pages.explain: **¡Un aplauso para el asador!** Everyone claps, even if the meat was a bit dry.

pages.text: When the asador calls **“¡A comer!”** or **“¡A la mesa!”**, go right away. Letting the meat go cold while you finish a story is the real insult.
The asador cooked, so the others clear the table and wash up. Offer to help with the dishes: that's how you get invited back.

classes.title: Asados from the rest of the country
classes.summary: Lamb on a cross, beef in its hide and dinner in a plough disc

pages.text: Down south the star isn't beef. It's **cordero patagónico**: a whole lamb opened flat, wired to an iron cross and stuck in the ground beside the fire for hours. On menus it's **cordero a la cruz** or **al asador**.
The big-party version is **asado con cuero**: beef cooked with its hide on. The hide works like a pot, holding in the juices and fat.

pages.prompt: A festival poster says the **vaquillona con cuero** is served at 1 p.m. When did the cooks light the fire?
pages.explain: Twelve hours or more over the embers means starting the night before and taking turns. Someone always brings a guitar and a termo.

pages.text: The town of **Viale**, in Entre Ríos, throws a national festival for asado con cuero every year.
In the west it's **chivito**: young goat, grilled slowly over the embers, a specialty of Mendoza and Neuquén. Further north it's called **cabrito**.

pages.prompt: Out in the **campo** there's a giant pan for the fire called **el disco**. What was it originally?
options: A plough disc from the farm
The rim of a cart wheel
pages.explain: A worn-out **disco de arado**, plough disc, with legs and handles welded on. Instant giant wok.

pages.text: Chicken, onions, peppers, chorizo and a splash of wine, all stewing together: **pollo al disco**. One disco feeds a crowd, everyone standing around it with bread.

sections.title: Fútbol
sections.summary: Clubs, chants, Maradona, Messi and Monday's teasing

classes.title: ¿De qué cuadro sos?
classes.summary: The question you can't dodge, and the rivalries behind it

pages.text: Meet someone in Argentina and within ten minutes you'll hear it: **¿De qué cuadro sos?** Which team are you? Here a club is a **cuadro**.
Five clubs are **los cinco grandes**: Boca, River, Independiente, Racing and San Lorenzo. Everyone else is a “small” club. Just don't say that to their fans.
The biggest match of all is **Boca vs River**: the **Superclásico**. Two clubs that hate each other more than anything.

pages.prompt: So where was River born?
options: In La Boca, right next to Boca
In Núñez, where it plays today
pages.explain: Both clubs started in La Boca. River moved north later. Neighbors first, enemies forever.

pages.text: In 2018 they met in the Copa Libertadores final. Boca's bus was attacked on the way to the second leg, so the final was moved to **Madrid**. River won.

pages.prompt: Racing and Independiente are fierce rivals. How far apart are their stadiums?
pages.explain: You can see one stadium from the other. That's the **clásico de Avellaneda**: living three blocks from the team you hate most.

pages.text: Golden rule: never wear one club's colors near the other's stadium. Especially on match day.

Want to go to a match? Boca and River tickets go mostly to **socios**, club members. Away fans were banned in 2013 and are only slowly coming back. And keep away from the **barra brava**, the organised hard-core fans.
No team? Don't fake one. Say **“De ninguno todavía. ¿Vos de cuál sos?”** (None yet. Which one are you?) and enjoy the next half hour of stories.

classes.title: La hinchada
classes.summary: Jumping stadiums, rock-song chants, cábalas and mufas

pages.text: A fan is a **hincha**. The whole crowd is **la hinchada**. They don't watch the match. They play it from the stands.
You don't pick a club. **You're born into it.** Lots of babies are signed up as club members before they can walk.

pages.prompt: Boca fans say their stadium, La Bombonera, “doesn't shake, it beats”, like a heart. Why?
options: The whole crowd jumps at the same time
It was built over an old stream
The club plays drums through the speakers
pages.explain: When the whole stadium jumps together, the stands really move. **“La Bombonera no tiembla, late.”**

pages.text: The singing never stops, and lots of the songs are old rock hits with new words. **“Brasil, decime qué se siente”** is sung to *Bad Moon Rising*.
Every rival gets a nickname. River fans call Boca fans **bosteros** (bosta = dung). Boca fans call River fans **gallinas**: chickens.

pages.prompt: Why are River fans called “gallinas”?
options: River was winning 2–0 in a big final and lost
Their first stadium was a chicken farm
Their old shirt had feathers on it
pages.explain: In the 1966 Copa Libertadores final, River were winning 2–0 and lost 4–2. At the next match, rival fans threw a chicken onto the pitch. The name stuck.

pages.text: Hinchas are superstitious. Same seat, same socks, the shirt you never wash: that's a **cábala**. And if your team loses every time you show up, you're **mufa**: bad luck.

pages.prompt: Your friend's team lost the last 3 matches you watched together. Tonight is the big one. What happens?
options: He saves you the best spot on the couch
He asks you to watch it somewhere else
He lends you his lucky shirt
pages.explain: Nothing personal: you're **mufa**. Maybe you can come back next season.

pages.text: Your team loses, it rains, the stadium is far away. You go anyway, and you sing louder. That loyalty has a name: **aguante**.

classes.title: Talk like a hincha
classes.summary: The potrero, the weekly picado, the previa and Monday's gastada

pages.text: Argentines say their football was born in the **potrero**: a dirt lot, two stones for goals, no rules. Calling a player **“de potrero”** is a big compliment.
Today the potrero is **fútbol 5**. Plenty of adults play a **picado** every week, with the same friends for years. Then beers.

pages.prompt: In a picado, you play the ball past your friend Nacho and everyone screams **“¡Caño!”**. What did you just do?
options: Put the ball between his legs
Kicked him instead of the ball
pages.explain: A **caño** is a nutmeg. No goal needed: Nacho will hear about it for weeks.

pages.text: Everyday words: the stadium is **la cancha**, the goalkeeper is the **arquero**, a great goal is a **golazo**. To ask the result: **¿Cómo salió?** Then **ganamos**, **perdimos** or **empatamos**: we won, we lost, we drew.
The coach is **el DT**, the director técnico. And every Argentine is secretly a DT: they all know who should have played.
Before a big match you **hacés la previa**: meet early to eat, drink and sing. The previa often lasts longer than the match.

pages.prompt: It's Monday. Your team lost 4–0 yesterday. What's waiting for you at the office?
options: Nobody mentions it, out of respect
Memes, jokes, and a rival's shirt on your chair
pages.explain: That's the **gastada**: the teasing you get after your team loses.

pages.text: The **gastada** is the teasing after a loss. You take it, you save the memes, and you pay it back when you win. “It's only a game” is not an accepted answer.

classes.title: Relegation, promedios and VAR
classes.summary: Irse a la B, the promedios and endless penalty debates

pages.text: Every club's nightmare is the **descenso**: relegation. Argentines call it **irse a la B**, going down to the B. Even giants fall.

pages.prompt: Four of the big five clubs have been relegated. Which one never has?
pages.explain: Boca has never gone down. Their fans never let anyone forget it.

pages.text: River went down in 2011, probably the biggest shock in Argentine football history. Boca fans still sing about it. River fans answer with one word: Madrid.

pages.prompt: Your team finished fifth this season, but your friend is still scared of going down. How is that possible?
options: Bad seasons from years ago still count
The top five teams swap leagues
The VAR can take points away
pages.explain: Clubs can go down on their **promedio**: an average of the last three seasons, so old bad years still count.

pages.text: The **promedio** is a club's points per match over the last three seasons. Today two clubs go down: the last in the year's table and the last in the promedios. Critics say the system protects the big clubs.
Every close call goes to **el VAR**, and the debate lasts until Thursday: **¿fue penal?** Was it a penalty? Old-timers still yell **orsai**: offside, the way their grandparents said it.

classes.title: Diego, 1986 and the pioneers
classes.summary: A World Cup with a shadow, a church for Diego, and the women who beat England first

pages.text: When **la Selección** plays, the country stops. Boca and River fans hug when Argentina scores. Three World Cups so far: 1978, 1986 and 2022. In 2026 it lost the final to Spain.
1978 was won at home, under a military dictatorship that used the cup as propaganda. Many Argentines still feel uneasy celebrating it. If it comes up, listen more than you talk.
**Diego Maradona** grew up poor in Villa Fiorito and became the country's biggest idol. His face is painted on walls all over Buenos Aires.

pages.prompt: Some fans founded a “church” for Maradona. When do they celebrate Christmas?
options: June 22, the day he beat England
pages.explain: The **Iglesia Maradoniana** started in Rosario in 1998 and counts its years from his birth, in 1960. June 22 is its Easter. Half joke, half not.

pages.text: People call him **el Diez**, the number ten, or just **el Diego**. He died on November 25, 2020. The wake was at the Casa Rosada, and huge crowds came to say goodbye.

Mexico 1986, quarter-final against England at the Azteca stadium, four years after the **Malvinas** (Falklands) war. Diego scores with his hand, **la Mano de Dios**, then dribbles past half their team. Argentina went on to win the cup.

pages.prompt: Diego wasn't the first Argentine to beat England at that same stadium. Who was?
pages.explain: In 1971, at an unofficial women's World Cup, Argentina's women beat England 4–1 at the Azteca.

pages.text: **Elba Selva** scored all four goals that day. August 21 is now the **Día de la Futbolista**, the Day of the Woman Footballer.

classes.title: Messi and Qatar
classes.summary: Heartbreak in Brazil, glory in Qatar, one more final in 2026

pages.text: **Messi** grew up in Rosario and left for Barcelona at 13. For years, some Argentines complained that he only played well for Barça.

pages.prompt: Why did Messi move to Barcelona as a kid?
options: Barça paid for his growth treatment
His dad got a job in Spain
